items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I seek
your guidance and clarification around a previous ruling by Speaker Wilson, 188/4,
which says that when a question is asked of a member, there can be one or, perhaps, two
supplementary questions on that primary. Yesterday, in your position, the Deputy
Speaker appeared to rule that from now on there would be only one supplementary
question, and it must be asked by the same member who asked the primary.
I think this is important for the House because if his ruling is to be taken as the way
forward, it means that members, as we saw yesterday, can put on an endless number of
questions to members that have no possibility of being hijacked by a hostile
supplementary q uestion and, effectively, put on a dog and pony show for political
purposes and, frankly, waste the House’s time.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: Speaking to the point of order, notwithstanding
the validity of that point of order, Speaker’s ruling 188/1 says that: “No member has an
absolute right to be given the call to ask a supplementary question.”

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And I appreciate that both members are focused on page 18 8 of
Speakers’ Rulings . I will give further consideration to the matter. It is actually a
question that I raised in a review of the Standing Orders at a Standing Orders
Committee hearing today, because I think there is little value in a line of questioning
such as we had yesterday, with members just using it simply to promote a member’s
bill. It is a matter for further discussion at the Standing Orders Committee, but, in the
meantime, I think the member David Seymour makes a reasonable point about what the
value of such a line of questions is and the patsy answers, frankly, that were given in the
House yesterday. I will give it further consideration.
Emergency Housing—Supply
1. PHIL TWYFORD (Labour —Te Atatū)  to the Minister for Social Housing :
Does she stand by her statement on emergency housing, “We are on track to have 8,600
places across the country available. We want to have the bulk of those in place  by this
winter”; if so, can she guarantee there won’t be more families living in cars and garages
this winter?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Yes; and no.
17478 Oral Questions 13 Apr 2017

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Were the emergency housing providers wrong when they warned
recently that more homeless families will be sleeping in cars, parks, and garages in
Auckland this winter because of a desperate shortage of affordable rentals?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: What I would say is that this Government has recognised that
there is a need for more emergency and transitional housing places to help people in
insecure housing, which is why we committed $354 million to doing something no
Government has ever done, which is to provide Government assistance to build 2,150
more emergency and transitional social housing places, which will house up to 8,600
households every year. That is a significant improvement on the situation prior to this
Government.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: How is it that by March this year only a third of the emergency
housing places she promised were actually available —only five more beds than in
September last year?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: That is because these have to b e new houses. The Ministry of
Social Development teams are in the market looking flat out for every available piece of
land and every available provider. We have the money available, but we have to find the
real estate, and building and bringing new houses  to market does not happen quickly.
We are moving at pace. Over the period the member quotes, we have actually delivered
90 new places, but as some contracts have come to a close, that has seen the net number
change. As I have said, we are on track to have  the bulk of our new places available for
winter.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Well, where are the new beds going to come from, given that she has
in the pipeline only enough to deliver half of what she promised in September, with
only 143 more properties contracted to be provided by NGOs before winter?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: I dispute the member’s characterisation, because, actually, our
indications are that we are well on track to have at least 1,700 of those 2,100 in place for
this winter, and we  are working hard to ensure even more are in place for this winter.
That is the commitment we have made —to have the bulk of them in place —and I have
every confidence that we will do that.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Why has the Government failed to follow  through on its promises,
after thousands of people endured a winter of misery last year and now we head into
another winter with a housing market that is still acutely short of affordable rentals?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: The Government has not fail ed to deliver on its promises. In
fact, it has done exactly what it promised to do, which was to put $354 million of new
money into funding an area that has never been funded previously, to build 2,150 places
across New Zealand, which will house 8,600 fami lies every year. We are well on track
to have the bulk of those in place by this winter. That is exactly what we promised. We
are doing it, and it is something that the Labour Government failed to do in all its time
in office, despite clear evidence of need.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Does she regret, after 8 years of her Government denying that there is
a housing crisis, that she, as the Minister, is now having to deal with the human cost of
her colleagues’ failed housing policy?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Well, we are absolutely clear that there is a need for
emergency and transitional funding, which is why we are putting $354 million into it.

items.speaker: But let us be clear
items.text: this is not a new problem. What is new is that this is a Government
that is actually do ing something about it. Whether it is through Minister Smith’s land
use development proposals or bringing on available capability, this is a Government that
is backing development, while Labour did nothing in its time in office and is now
opposing housing developments.

items.speaker: Hon Michael Woodhouse
items.text: What reports has she seen of people living in cars?
13 Apr 2017 Oral Questions 17479

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: I have seen reports from the Bay of Plenty Times  of people
sleeping in cars and under trees, and of the Salvation Army turning people away. I have
seen stories from the New Zealand Herald  of Monte Cecilia turning people away from
homes, who end up in cars and garages, because there is no room; from the Salvation
Army, of people living in  shanty towns similar to those in Brazil and the Philippines,
and of people living in Northland in cars because they are unable to afford housing. All
of those were from 2004 and 2005, when Labour did nothing.
Greenhouse Gas Emissions—Minister's Response to GLOBE-NZ’s Report
2. JAMES SHAW (Co -Leader—Green) to the Minister for Climate Change

items.speaker: Issues
items.text: Does the Government agree with th e conclusions and recommendations in the

items.speaker: Vivid report Net Zero in New Zealand
items.text: Scenarios to achieve domestic emissions
neutrality in the second half of the century?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I think the Vivid
Economics report is a valuable contribution to the debate about how best to tackle
climate change, but it looks very long term and also does not set out the costs of the
various forms of reducing or offsetting emissions that it suggests. We need to look at
that before we will know the combination of policies that will be best for New Zealand.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: Does she agree with the first conclusion —that staying within 2
degrees of global warming will require New Zealand getting to 98 percent renewable
energy by 2050, as well as an 85 percent uptake of electric vehicles?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: We already have a target of 90 percent renewable energy,
which, compared with other countries, is very high. I am advised that anything above 90
percent will mean we would need to have a lot more backup generation available. So
whilst I do not disagree, I am also excited about technology improvements that perhaps
might come as well.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: Does she agree with the second conclusion —that staying within 2
degrees of global warming will require an alteration to our land -use patterns, even if all
of the scientific and technological research on reducing anim al emissions is successful
and fully implemented?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I certainly agree that we need to plant more trees and that
that is an important part of tackling climate change in the future, but we simply do not
know what technolo gical advances there will be in that case. We will be making them,
in the next decades, on agricultural emission.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: Does she agree with the report’s first recommendation —that a higher,
more predictable price on emissions would help t o avoid locking in high emissions
infrastructure that makes it impossible to get to a low -emission economy—and would
she consider removing the current $25 a tonne price cap?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: To the first part, yes, and that is why we removed the
“two for one”. We have already seen the first third come off and that people will be
paying the full emissions. As far as the cap is concerned, that is part of the emissions
trading scheme (ETS), phase two, and that is being considered.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: Would she agree with recommendation two —that putting a price on
biological emissions from agriculture would encourage land -use decisions that take
emissions intensity into account?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I do not believe w e should be bringing agriculture into
the ETS at this time. As I have said, we need to balance the need to reduce emissions
with the fact that our farmers are so important to global food supply and, in fact, at this
time feed more than 40 million people around the world.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: Does she agree with recommendation nine —that an area for further
policy development is addressing the distributional implications of differing low
17480 Oral Questions 13 Apr 2017
emissions scenarios; in other words, adjust transition to protect pe ople’s incomes and
livelihoods?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Yes, I do. I do agree with that. I think we need to look at
what the offsets are, what the real costs are, and how we can get that right balance.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: Does she agree with recommendation six—for an independent climate
commission based on the UK model to guide policy settings towards a net zero carbon
economy?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: No, I do not agree with that at this time. I think the UK
was in a different place on climate change when it did it. But I must say that this report
and the work that is going on with Global New Zealand  lead us to more of an all -of-
Parliament approach, which I think is really important for this debate.
Mixed-ownership Companies—Performance

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Question No. 3—Chris Bishop.

items.speaker: CHRIS BISHOP
items.text: Oh, thank you very much, Mr Speaker. Sorry, I was
just enraptured by the climate change question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! We will just have the question.
3. CHRIS BISHOP (National)  to the Minister of Finance : How are the mixed -
ownership companies performing under their new ownership structures?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The mixed -ownership compan ies
are performing very well. The aggregate dividends from the electricity companies to the
Crown have increased by 39 percent since listing. They have not dropped by 49 percent,
as you might expect, due to the Crown listing 49 percent of the shares. For e xample, the
Crown is now receiving more than twice as much in dividends from Genesis Energy
than it did pre-listing, even though we own only 51 percent of the company. While it is
impossible to work out exactly how much the mixed -ownership structure has im pacted
on these dividends, it is clear that the greater commercial discipline, as a result of being
listed companies, is working to the benefit of taxpayers as well as to mum and dad
investors.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: How has the value of these mixed -ownership companies changed
during this time?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The value of the mixed -ownership electricity companies
has increased by around 4 percent since June 2012. In addition, Air New Zealand’s
market capitalisation has increased significantly over time to over $2.5 billion today.
During this period, that company too has paid growing dividends on the back of
improving performance. So the value of these mixed -ownership companies has
increased, the amount of dividends paid has increa sed, and that has given the
Government additional choices to address specific priorities with the dividends that we
have received.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: How have retail electricity prices tracked given the greater
commercial pressures on the “gentailers”?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: This is very interesting, actually, because a lot of people
assume that that means prices must have gone up, but, actually, prices have been
remarkably flat at this moment. According to the quarterly survey of do mestic
electricity prices, the retail price per kilowatt hour has increased by less than 1c over the
last 3 years and by only 25 percent over the last 8 years. That compares with prices
hiking 65 percent under the previous Government. New Zealand families are better off
due to stable electricity prices as well as receiving those improved dividends through
the Government’s direct investments.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: How has electricity supply and demand responded to New Zealand’s
strongly growing economy?
13 Apr 2017 Oral Questions 17481

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Speaking of patsies that achieve nothing.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I would listen carefully if I were you, Mr Hipkins —you are
learning something. New Zealand’s economy has experienced  15 quarters of
consecutive growth and is one of the fastest growing economies in the OECD. Despite
this, New Zealand is actually consuming less electricity than it was 10 years ago. This is
a testament to the innovation of New Zealanders and a focus on gr eater energy
efficiency. In addition, the share of renewables is also climbing. In 2006 two -thirds of
our power was renewable electricity; last year that was 85 percent. It has to be said that
this progress would be put at risk if policy decision makers were to change direction and
introduce policies to disregard the market, as was advocated in the last election.
Education, Minister—Record
4. CHRIS HIPKINS (Labour —Rimutaka) to the Minister of Education : Which
of the following best describes her tenure as Minister of Education: her abandoned plan
to increase class sizes, her proposed Christchurch school closures, her closure of
residential special schools, the introduction of charter schools, the decline in
international achievement ratings, or the roll-out of Novopay?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. May I
thank the member for not surprising me and not being able to rise above that
gracelessness. What I think this list demonstrates about my tenure as Minister of
Education is that I have always been prepared to make the tough decisions  that are in
the best interests of our young people, rather than what might be easiest for adults. What
I think better describes my tenure —for which I feel most privileged —is what has been
my relentless focus on our children and young people. That has been  characterised by
this: all of our young students now are starting earlier, staying longer, and leaving better
qualified. That is reflected in student stand downs, suspensions, and exclusions being at
the lowest levels since records began 16 years ago. Sin ce 2011 the rate of children
starting school has reached almost 98 percent, provisional results for 18 -year-olds have
them at 85.2 percent, and we have invested in a quality agenda to support our teachers
to grow their teaching practice. We have invested $ 359 million in educational success,
197 communities of learning have been established, involving over half a million young
people, and—I am about to finish —we have increased Vote Education from $8 billion
to $11 billion, which is the most any Government ha s ever invested. I am proud of my
tenure.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Will she now, in her final question time as Minister of Education,
finally apologise to the schools, teachers, and families in Christchurch who, having been
shepherded into a hall and  given colour-coded name tags, discovered halfway through
the meeting that the colour of their name tag denoted whether she intended to close,
merge, or leave open their schools?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I can attest to a much better approach t han what the
member commends. I went down to Christchurch, community by community, and
apologised in person to them. Then I set about making a case to this Government to
secure over a billion dollars to rebuild and renew so that the Greater Christchurch,
Waimakariri, and Selwyn areas would have the best 21 st century education network in
this country and, indeed, in Australasia. I am satisfied that I have made well on that one
mistake.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Will she now apologise to teachers and sch ool staff for approving
the implementation of Novopay, despite the trials having proven it did not pay staff
properly, and the advice to her at the time was that there were 147 known faults with the
system?
17482 Oral Questions 13 Apr 2017

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I think that  the apology from this Government —including
myself—was to take action as quickly as possible and to absolutely empathise and
sympathise, because no Government wants to see anyone losing their salary because of
a digital failure. Together, with my colleague  the Hon Steven Joyce, we worked hard to
rectify that, and now the error rate is lower than the previous system, and is certainly
lower than that member’s.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Will she now apologise to the families and students at Salisbury
School for her first failed attempt to close the school, which Justice Dobson called “an
abrogation of the responsibilities involved in making a decision”, and given Justice
Dobson’s conclusion that “No great leap of logic [was] required to recognise the
validity of concerns”?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: In respect of Salisbury School in particular, there is a
process that we are in the middle of, and we will continue that process because that is
what the law provides for. In terms of special education  learning support for those
young people most vulnerable, with clinical or behavioural disorders, this Government
has increased funding by 29 percent. Under my watch we have introduced the Intensive
Wraparound Service, which has seen many more young people  being given support so
they can live comfortably in their own communities. Residential hostels have their
place, but in these modern times it is far more sustainable to find ways to help those
young people be successful in their own home communities.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Does she regret the breakdown in her relationship with Lesley
Longstone, the former Secretary for Education, who left with a $425,000 golden
handshake as a result?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: The member misremembers. The re was no breakdown in
our relationship. The particular appointee was unable to meet the requirements, and that
has been demonstrated by subsequent appointments in the form of Peter Hughes, now
chief commissioner, and in the current form of Iona Holsted —both eminently capable
of carrying out these roles and discharging them very effectively.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Is she proud of the fact that the two major international Programme
for International Student Assessment (PISA) studies released during h er time as
Minister of Education both showed Kiwi kids getting worse in their literacy, worse in
their numeracy, and worse in their science?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I am proud of the New Zealand education system. It is one
that has constantly striven to improve itself. What the PISA results tell us and caution us
about is that we have constantly got to improve. We do not resile from those, but then
they are triangulated with the national student monitoring project out of the University
of Otago , by the Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study and the
Progress in International Reading Literacy Study, and by the best evidence synthesis.
So, unlike the member, we do not hang off one international study because it happens to
support a member’s point of view; we look at the round, and what we see and should be
proud of is the achievement of young New Zealanders. So, yes, I am proud of them.
Police Resourcing—Numbers
5. RON MARK (Deputy Leader—NZ First) to the Prime Minister: Does he have
confidence in his Minister of Police; if so, why?
Hon PAULA BENNETT (Deputy Prime Minister)  on behalf of the Prime

items.speaker: Minister
items.text: Yes; and for too many reasons to go into at this point.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Further to the Prime Minister’s answer to my primary question
yesterday, when the Minister of Police expl ained the roll -out of the policy to increase
police numbers, how many new police officers did she tell him would be on duty on 1
July 2018—would it be 220 or 2?
13 Apr 2017 Oral Questions 17483

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: The Prime Minister would not have that level of detail a t
the top of his head. You should put that question to the Minister of Police.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The question actually asked that
when the Minister of Police briefed him, did she tell him—and there was the rest of it. It
was about the discussion—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s question has been addressed. If he wishes to
continue with supplementary questions, I would suggest he tighten them up a bit, and
then we can help him.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: Why did he agree to fund only 880 sworn officers when advice from
the New Zealand Police itself was that it would need 1,165 sworn officers to “lift police
visibility across the country, halt the rise in crime, reduce social harm, and provide
additional reassurance and capacity across rural New Zealand and Auckland.”?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Papers that were presented by the then Minister of Police
prior to December last year put forward three different proposals. One was for fewer
police than what we put forward, one was for more, and one was at the number that we
have landed on. Once digging in, the 1,125 police are what we consider will address the
needs of New Zealand at this time and for the next 4 years.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Did the Ministe r of Police tell him that of the 880 extra police 116
would be youth aid, 66 would be dedicated to family violence, leaving only 698 front -
line general duty officers to deal with the ever -increasing numbers of bashings,
burglaries, robberies, abductions, a nd car thefts; is that the hallmark of an effective
Minister of Police?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: There are two supplementary questions there. The Minister can
address one or both.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Yes, because I read the Cabinet paper,  which is where
that member got that information from, and that is exactly what was in it.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: How can he have confidence in his Minister of Police when she has told
him that only 20 police stations will have 24/7 policing coverage, leaving  271 police
stations around the country that will not have 24/7 coverage?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Because, actually, the member is counting all 300 police
stations, and it might be of interest to him that a number of them are already 24/7. S o
the 20 that were announced yesterday are in addition to the 24/7 stations that are
currently there.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: How can the Prime Minister have confidence in his Minister of Police
when at the same time she is saying that she is increasing police  numbers, she has
allowed the culling of something between 111 and 200 police road -safety staff,
including highway patrol? When is she going to come clean and admit to the House that
those redundancies have happened?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Because the member has simply got his facts wrong.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! A point of order has been raised, and the point of order will
be heard in silence.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Thank you. Then, for the benefit—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I will just have the point of order, please.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: I seek leave to table a statement from the Police Association saying that
there was a $26 million dispute—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I just want the source of the statement.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: From the Police Association.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is it a public press release from the Police Association?

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: I have no idea. I just got it this afternoon.
17484 Oral Questions 13 Apr 2017

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member should do further homework before he seeks leave to
table such documents.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: I seek leave to table a document that is a ministerial discussion from
New Zealand Police titled Talking points on resource Cabinet paper , dated 21
December 2016, where the Police state that they need 1,165 sworn police for prevention
to change the trajectory—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am receiving interjections that that is publicly available.
Can the member confirm that?

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: Is it publicly available? So everyone knows—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And I am not putting the leave if it is publicly available.
Greenhouse Gas Emissions—Minister's Response to GLOBE-NZ’s Report
6. Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM (Green) to the Minister for Climate Change Issues:
Which of the four scenarios in the March 2017 Vivid report —“Off Track”,
“Innovative”, “Resourceful”, or “Net Zero 2050”—is the Government considering using
as the basis for its own climate planning?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.role: Minister for Climate C hange Issues
items.text: The Vivid report
is a welcome addition to the debate and it outlines, as the member says, a number of
scenarios that New Zealand could follow to reduce emissions. I believe there is more
work to be done on the basis of that report, and I thi nk it is a really good start, but we
would have to do more work to decide which track we would go down, or whether there
might be others.

items.speaker: Dr Kennedy Graham
items.text: Does the Minister agree with the fourth conclusion in the
report—that if substa ntial afforestation is combined with extensive technological
innovation, it could be possible to achieve domestic net zero emissions by 2050?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I do not have a crystal ball. So it is hard for me to say —
[Interruption] So it is difficult for me to say what will be happening in 2050 and what
those technological advances could be, but I have to say that I am hopeful.

items.speaker: Dr Kennedy Graham
items.text: What steps will she consider taking from here to strengthen
the relationship between GLOBE-NZ and the executive in light of recommendation No.
5 of the report?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I am very supportive of the work that GLOBE -NZ has
done. Can I acknowledge the member for his tireless effort to have cross-party work.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Hear, hear!

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: —yeah, he does deserve that —and that the National
Party, through the work that Scott Simpson is leading for us on this side, has got a
number of members and is committed to  it. I, as Minister, am interested in an ongoing
involvement.

items.speaker: Dr Kennedy Graham
items.text: If GLOBE -NZ were to commission a follow -up study to
explore in more depth the “net zero 2050” scenario, would the Government be prepared
to seriously consider such an analysis?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I would not be prepared to commit to that right now, but I
certainly do not want to rule it out completely, either. We would have to see the terms
of what that might be.
NCEA—Results for 2016
7. SARAH DOWIE (National—Invercargill) to the Minister of Education: What
recent announcements has she made regarding NCEA results?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Earlier
today I was pleased to announce the final NCEA results for 2016. These latest results
are by far the best we h ave seen since we came into Government at the end of 2008,

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: I move, That the House note the report

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: The debate this afternoon marks the end of the Vivid
Economics project and the beginning of something new in New Zealand climate policy.
I thank all the members of GLOBE -NZ for their collegial engagement, especially the
executive committee of  the Hon Peter Dunne, Marama Fox, Tracey Martin, Scott
Simpson, and Dr Megan Woods. I give appreciation, of course, to the Minister and to
yourself, Mr Speaker, for your high levels of interest and support.
The Vivid Economics report reflects unprecedented  cross-party collaboration. It
provides an opportunity for developing an ambitious pathway to domestic emissions
neutrality, as called for in the Paris Agreement. Nothing is more critical to the fate of
New Zealand and the well -being of future generations.  I think the very fact that this
debate is being held testifies to that. May I pay tribute to the Vivid Economics team in

items.speaker: London
items.text: John Ward, Alex Kazaglis, and Paul Sammon, who now know New Zealand
better than they ever dreamt they would. I also pay tribut e to their broader team in
London as well, and, of course, the donors here in New Zealand for making it possible,
and may I single out Sir Stephen Tindall, who led in that respect. Finally, I pay tribute
to Catherine Leining, our Wellington-based consultant, to whom we all owe a huge vote
of thanks.
James Shaw will convey the Green Party’s initial views on the report itself. I shall
confine myself to a broader observation, which is, perhaps, more a Green perspective on
the shared vision that is GLOBE -NZ. I do so because, only weeks after its release and
with an election ahead, we must none the less ask ourselves: where to from here? The
report identifies four scenarios for achieving emissions neutrality, three of which would
achieve the goal in the second ha lf of the century as the Paris Agreement calls for. We
shall no doubt be discussing with our cross -party group which of these, or which
13 Apr 2017 Special Debates 17491
combination of them, might have the most policy merit, for, ultimately, we need to
move from scenarios to policy. The te ctonic tension in this respect will be over two
broad considerations: the speed with which we must move, on the one hand, and the
need for economic stability and distributional justice as we go —the imperative of
urgency and the art of transition. We shall all have our views.

items.speaker: From my personal perspective I think the following
items.text: I have been working on climate
change since 1989. The first Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change report of 1990
and the Rio convention of 1992 made clear the consequences of dang erous climate
change and the need to avoid it. Since then our annual global emissions have risen
hugely and so have our national emissions. We have lost a quarter of a century through
largely ineffectual old -style negotiations, which we pursue in short -term, competitive,
zero-sum style. That is not the way to solve 21 st century global commons problems. I
say this more in sorrow than in anger. We are where we are. But it leaves us with a far
higher gradient of challenge than when we started and we have very little time left. It
was only yesterday that Christiana Figueres, former UN climate head and now UN
climate ambassador, identified 2020 as the year in which global carbon emissions must
peak for the 2 degree goal in the Paris Agreement to be realised.
So where to from here for New Zealand? I believe the report will be invaluable in
facilitating cross-party policy debate—and throughout the country. In particular, I hope
that we can pursue in more depth the challenge posed in scenario four of the report:
neutrality by 2050. I know this will be difficult, but I know it also to be an imperative
and a broader challenge to place domestic neutrality in the context of New Zealand’s
overall national responsibility level within the finite and diminishing global carbon
budget.
So let us continue our discussions informally around the table and see how far and
how fast we can proceed, blending short -term and longer-term responsibilities because,
ultimately, they are one and the same, and, ultimately, we are all in this ex traordinary
saga together.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: Might I start my contribution on
this momentous debate with a  message to the good people of Coromandel, who, this
afternoon, have bearing down upon them the remains of Cyclone Cook. My advice is to
go home and stay home. Do not go out onto the roads unless it is absolutely necessary.
My best wishes are with you. Loo k after your neighbours. I am heading home as fast as
I can.
Across the House this is a momentous debate. The popular perception of this
Parliament is that MPs constantly work in an adversarial manner, constantly batting
their sharp tongues and their poli cy initiatives against each other, constantly trying to
score points and constantly trying to outwit and outmatch each other. Much of that
occurs to the absolute bemusement of most New Zealand voters. This report —this very
fine Vivid report —is an example o f our Parliament working, I think, at its very best.
That 35 members of this Parliament —representative of every party in this House —
could come together to embark upon a project of common interest, of shared interest in
climate change and climate change issues, is, I think, a historic and momentous event.
I wish to thank Dr Kennedy Graham, who chairs the New Zealand chapter of
GLOBE International. I want to thank my parliamentary colleagues, I want to thank the
funders who have made this report possible, an d I want to thank, of course, the Vivid
team, which has actually produced it.
This report is actually Vivid’s report. This is not our report as MPs. This does not
belong to one particular party. This is a report that, I hope, many New Zealanders will
read, will think about, will debate, and will engage with in an active, informed
17492 Special Debates 13 Apr 2017
conversation about the options that we as a country might take in order to fulfil our
ambitious Paris Agreement obligations.
It is appropriate that parties will and should have different policy perspectives. There
will be differences across this Parliament about how we might, as a party or as a
Government or as a nation, achieve those climate change commitments that we as a
nation have signed up to. That is good and proper. That is as it should be, because there
will be differences in tone, there will be differences in focus, and there will be
differences in the pace and speed of initiatives that are going to be required to achieve
those targets. That is something that we should n ot shy away from; it is something that
we should not shirk from.
This report, and the various scenarios that are enunciated in it and are given up for
debate and discussion, are all long term. We have got ourselves, as a world, into this
situation over a l ong period of time, and it is going to take us a long period of time to
change the direction in which we are going, in which we are traveling. Some would say
that we do not have much time, and I am of that opinion, so I am very fascinated by the
various scenarios that are presented to us.
Although this piece of work starts the conversation, the actual impacts, the cost, the
implementations, and the fine detail remain unanswered. This piece of work is a
beginning of a conversation. It is a beginning of a deb ate in this Parliament. It is a
beginning of a debate that we should be having as a nation. It is not an end piece in its
own right. So I hope that, as a result of this very good report, there will be widespread
discussion, there will be widespread debate amongst politicians, amongst any New
Zealander who has an interest in the future of the globe and the future of New Zealand’s
environment and our place and part in both those important areas.
I want to acknowledge the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for  Climate Changes
Issues, the Hon Paula Bennett. I think this Minister brings to this debate a remarkable
communication skill. In her own inimitable style and way, she is able to bring to this
issue of climate change a vocabulary and a style that I think is  important if we are, as a
nation, to grasp the imagination and the hearts of middle New Zealand. And so I am
very pleased that she has been so involved in this process right from the beginning, and
I am looking forward to hearing her later on.
This Government’s focus is on how to transition to a low -carbon economy while still
promoting jobs, incomes, and a growing economy. This report, I think, is the foundation
stone of a starting point of a national, nationwide debate, and I commend it to the House
and to all New Zealanders.

others—because those leaders participated. Again, this is what has given us this really

My colleague Denis O’Rourke will speak in more depth to New Zealand First’s
response to the contents of the report, but we do have the capacity. I wou ld tend to
personally agree with Kennedy Graham that we need to be looking at neutrality by
2050, and I believe we have, and I am going to recommend the science dinners to every
member of Parliament. The numbers need to go up there, people, because the Nat ional
Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research has done some amazing work, funded by
the people of New Zealand, that will help us around soil saturation, the best use of
pasteurisation, and where we can go from here.
We need to have a wider conversation—and this will inform it—around the spread of
electric vehicles and the policy constraints and the policy constructions. Is it more
charging stations that actually take away distance anxiety? Is it low-cost loans that mean
more people can actually buy seco nd-hand electric vehicles? But how will we deal with
the fossil fuel vehicles that are then going to be dumped on to the side of the road? All
these conversations are now possible because of this report, and they are all possible
amongst us all because of GLOBE-NZ—because of what Kennedy Graham pulled
together out of this Parliament.
I also want to acknowledge the Speaker. The Speaker did not have to give permission
to have this debate. This is a special event, and I think he did so because he recognised
that for the New Zealand Parliament to come together in such a collaborative way is
unusual, and it is something that needs to be recognised and given this opportunity.
As I say, my colleague Denis O’Rourke will speak to it more, but we do want to
acknowledge that Vivid Economics came all the way out here. This was not a cheap
report, and it should not be, because downstream it is incredibly important to us as a
nation—as a trading nation —because it is going to become more and more important,
as everybody is going to want to know how we are participating in this particular issue.
I want to close by saying that I became more passionate about this issue when I
visited Tuvalu. We have a responsibility not only to our nation and to the planet, but we
really, really need to look to our Pacific neighbours and what our responsibility is in
trying to put a cap on what is happening there. Other conversations about climate
change refugees and so on will evolve downstream, but there is an immense urgency to
this issue, and some of it has to do with those who we must care about most, and those
are our Pasifika neighbours. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr
Assistant Speaker, kia ora tātou katoa. Can I just start by acknowledging all of the
acknowledgments made already by those who have been a part of this working party.
My colleague Marama Fox was certainly a part of it, and I have very much ap preciated
the involvement. Can I also acknowledge Kennedy Graham for driving this kaupapa. He
drove it so much that he forced me to make a statement in the House this afternoon on
behalf of our party. So thank you very much Kennedy, and I appreciate your
commitment to this kaupapa. Ka nui te mihi.
Issues about climate change are not things that I really know too much about. What I
do know about is the effect that it is having on communities at this point in time, in
particular in my rohe of Waiariki. I am thinking about those communities of
17494 Special Debates 13 Apr 2017
Edgecumbe, Ruātoki, and Ruatāhuna. As we debate this particular issue I send my
thoughts and, I am sure, those of the House back to those families and those kāinga
back at Waiariki and, indeed, throughout the country as we experience a not very nice
Easter weekend.
Governments of the world have agreed to limit average global warming to well
below 2 degrees Celsius. The Paris Agreement, which New Zealand ratified on 4
October 2016 and which came into force on 4 November 2 016, commits us and the
world to the so-called net zero goal by the end of the century, and puts in place a longer-
term framework to achieve this by agreeing to a new universal climate change
agreement. This new universal climate change agreement needs to set the world on a
clear path of a decline in emissions over time. The reality of the science indicates that
global emissions need to be halved by 2050, and, at some point in the second half of the
century, emissions need to be so low that healthy ecosyste ms such as forests can readily
absorb the emissions that are left.
A transformation to a climate -neutral, clean-energy economic model needs to occur
now. In those areas where it has begun it is already delivering huge benefits in and
between nations. Whil e the goal of the Paris Agreement is very clear, how different
countries achieve this is not so clear. The Vivid Economics report identified that for
New Zealand the transition to emission neutrality will require more than the current
practice. It will req uire changes in land use and pathways relying less on breakthrough
technologies and energy, and agriculture will require more extensive forestation by
It could be possible for New Zealand to reach net zero emissions by 2050 by
combining the high upt ake of technological innovation with a switch to less emissions -
intensive agricultural production, higher levels of forestation, and the end of energy -
intensive industries. Substantial gaps in New Zealand’s evidence base on domestic
mitigation must be addr essed to support well -informed decision -making in the future,
and the Māori Party wants to be a part of this.
However, the Māori Party believes that New Zealand’s ability to achieve domestic
emissions neutrality in the second half of the century and to me et its medium- and long-
term emission reduction obligations is fundamentally flawed, as current policies allow
for emitters to offset their obligations with low -cost credits without the need to reduce
emissions. Current policies incentivise major emitters who have been able to purchase
cheap Ukrainian units to surrender these to meet their obligations, while charging
Māori, and indeed New Zealand households, a huge, out-of-reach price for units.
We also believe that there has been some negligible investmen t in low -emission
technologies, resulting in foresters leaving the changed system, and planting is virtually
zero. This has a huge impact on Aotearoa, and also on those hapū and iwi who have
received large forests as a part of their Treaty settlements and so have large carbon
credits that are virtually worthless. This sort of statement has been made to me in the
Waiariki area.
So we welcome the Vivid report, which highlights our forestation as one way
forward. The Māori Party would want to see change withi n the climate area, as it has
also got huge implications socially, economically, and culturally, as well as
environmentally. The Māori Party is committed to ensuring New Zealand’s natural
resources and environment are healthy for everyone, and to supportin g the health and
well-being of our people. This requires that environmental degradation is addressed. We
believe New Zealand has time to transition to a low -emissions economy, but there are
benefits to taking strategic action and signalling long -term actions now. We support the
outcome of this report.
